enrichment.short_title: Whether section 49 anonymity ceases once a youth court defendant turns 18

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: T was 17 when charged with GBH after assaulting a court usher; he turned 18 during youth court proceedings and was sentenced to a four-month detention and training order.

After sentence the press applied for an order that section 49 no longer applied or, alternatively, for dispensation under section 49(4A); the magistrates held section 49 had fallen away on his 18th birthday.
The Sunderland Echo identified T the following day despite the pending case stated appeal.
The Divisional Court was asked whether reporting restrictions under section 49(1) cease once a defendant is no longer a child or young person.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from South Shields Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court (Administrative Court).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; answer to the magistrates' question was yes — section 49(1) no longer applied once T had attained 18.
enrichment.ratio: Section 49 protects only persons who remain children or young persons as defined in the Act; once a defendant concerned in youth court proceedings becomes 18, the automatic reporting prohibition in section 49(1) falls away, and subsections (4A) and (5) cannot sensibly be read as preserving anonymity for adults.
legal_issues: Whether section 49(1) applies throughout youth court proceedings even after the defendant turns 18
How section 49(1) interacts with the discretionary powers in sections 49(4A) and (5)
Whether proposed amendments in the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999 assist construction of the current provision
Whether Article 8 ECHR requires continued anonymity after adulthood

notes: Complete Court of Appeal ruling refusing preliminary applications for court-ordered civil legal representation.

enrichment.short_title: Litigant in person refused court-ordered representation on 23 permission-to-appeal applications
area_of_law: Legal aid and access to justice
key_facts: Angelo Perotti, an experienced litigant in person, listed 23 applications for permission to appeal arising from long-running estate administration, negligence, civil restraint, and related proceedings.

In each appellant's notice he sought first that the Court of Appeal provide legal representation under Article 6 and/or adjourn, and failing that permission to appeal so that pro bono representation would follow.
The court heard the preliminary representation issue with an advocate to the court appointed by the Attorney General.
Chadwick LJ held the court has no civil power comparable to criminal legal aid to direct representation, and Perotti could present his PTA applications without denial of effective access.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing on a preliminary question across multiple permission-to-appeal applications before merits determination.
enrichment.outcome: Applications in the terms of paragraph 1 of section 10 of application 2003/0552 and all similar applications refused; directions to follow for merits hearings; stay extended in related matter 2003/1662.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal has no power in civil proceedings to order legal representation or direct the Legal Services Commission to fund it; under Article 6(1) the threshold for requiring free representation in civil cases is high and is not met where a litigant can present permission-to-appeal points sufficiently for the court to assess real prospects of success.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal may order civil legal representation for a litigant in person
Whether Article 6(1) requires public funding for multiple permission-to-appeal applications
Relationship between Article 6(1) fair hearing and Article 6(3)(c) criminal legal aid
Whether refusal of representation would deny effective access to the courts

enrichment.short_title: Emergency section 4 MHA admission upheld despite form inconsistency on previous acquaintance
key_facts: On 19 September 2003 an approved social worker made an emergency section 4 application for admission of C for assessment based on one medical recommendation.
The social worker stated on the form that the patient was not known to a psychiatrist at the centre, while the medical practitioner did not delete the box indicating previous acquaintance.
A second medical recommendation was obtained within 72 hours; a tribunal hearing on 30 September was adjourned to 8 October after lengthy evidence.
C sought urgent interim release and judicial review, arguing the admission was unlawful and the tribunal adjournment breached Article 5.4.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent oral application for interim relief in judicial review, with permission to proceed determined at the same hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Permission for judicial review refused; interim relief refused; tribunal adjournment not unlawful.
enrichment.ratio: An apparent inconsistency between the social worker's and doctor's admission forms on whether the recommending practitioner had previous acquaintance with the patient does not render a section 4 admission unlawful where the doctor had examined the patient on the previous day; the Mental Health Review Tribunal's seven-day adjournment to complete a complex hearing was not a wrongful exercise of discretion under domestic law or Article 5.4.
legal_issues: Whether inconsistent completion of section 4 admission forms invalidated detention
Meaning of 'previous acquaintance' and 'if practicable' in section 4
Whether the tribunal could review legality of the original admission
Whether a seven-day adjournment breached Article 5.4 prompt determination requirement

enrichment.short_title: Auditors' negligence and Caparo duty claims against Ernst & Young survive strike-out
key_facts: Man Nutzfahrzeuge acquired ERF from Western Star/Freightliner for about £62 million in March 2000 relying on audited accounts later found to have been falsified by ERF financial controller Mr Ellis.
Man claimed very large losses; Freightliner's Part 20 claim against Ernst & Young Canada and Ernst & Young UK alleged negligent audits and failure properly to investigate tip-offs before completion.
EY applied to strike out the UK claim and set aside service out on the Canadian partnership for no reasonable prospect of success.
Cooke J held disputed Caparo, causation, and Galoo issues required trial and disclosure of audit working papers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in Commercial Court for strike out under CPR 3.4/24 and to set aside service out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Both EY applications dismissed; real issues to be tried; permission granted to amend the Part 20 claim subject to costs of amendment.
enrichment.ratio: On assumed pleaded facts, Freightliner had a real prospect of establishing that EYUK assumed responsibility to Western Star for audited accounts used in the ERF share sale and that losses were arguably caused by negligent failure to detect Ellis's fraud and follow up tip-offs; Galoo and Caparo points could not be resolved summarily without full factual investigation.
legal_issues: Whether auditors owed a duty beyond Caparo statutory purposes to a vendor shareholder in a specific sale
Scope of duties arising from due diligence and sale advisory engagements

Whether contribution claims under the 1978 Act were arguable

enrichment.short_title: Wall Street Journal libel meaning fixed at reasonable grounds to suspect terrorist ties
key_facts: Mohammed Abdul Latif Jameel and Abdul Latif Jameel Co Ltd sued over a 6 February 2002 Wall Street Journal (Europe) article about Saudi monitoring of bank accounts with potential terrorist ties.
At pre-trial review Eady J had to determine defamatory meaning and admissibility of eleven SAMA and Saudi bank witness statements served with Civil Evidence Act notices.
Both parties invited the court to delimit meaning before trial; there was no plea of justification.
The court also dealt with costs and abandonment of a separate internet publication claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Pre-trial review rulings in Queen's Bench libel action listed for trial in December 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Words held capable only of meaning there were reasonable grounds to suspect terrorist ties and funnelled funds; witness statements admissible to rebut Dorsey/Simpson evidence and support aggravated damages; internet claim costs to defendants; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a financial crime article focuses on accounts with potential terrorist ties, a fair-minded reader would not understand 'ties' or 'associations' at the lowest Chase tier of mere grounds to investigate; without justification, claimants may adduce evidence rebutting journalists' account of their sources and supporting aggravated damages without offending GKR Karate.
legal_issues: Whether the article bore Chase tier-one meaning of grounds merely to investigate
Whether pre-trial delimitation of meaning was appropriate
Admissibility of hearsay bank and SAMA statements where truth is presumed and there is no justification plea
Relevance of evidence to qualified privilege, source rebuttal, and aggravated damages

enrichment.short_title: Breath test conviction upheld despite operator's ignorance of calibration limits
key_facts: Haggis was stopped on 14 July 2002 and gave a lower breath reading of 43 microgrammes on a Camic Datamaster machine at Belle Vale police station.
PC Fagin, a trained operator, testified the machine was self-calibrating and working properly but accepted in cross-examination she did not know the correct calibration limits.
The printout was served on the defendant but not produced at the magistrates' hearing.
The deputy district judge convicted; the Divisional Court answered both case stated questions in favour of the prosecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Liverpool Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates could properly be satisfied the machine was operating correctly and PC Fagin was a trained operator.
enrichment.ratio: A police officer may be a trained breath-test operator notwithstanding imperfect knowledge of calibration limits; where a self-calibrating approved device produces a printout consistent with other evidence and nothing in the printout is shown to undermine reliability, the prosecution need not prove calibration figures on each occasion unless something raises doubt that the device tested itself properly.
legal_issues: Whether an operator who does not know calibration limits can prove the device was working properly
Whether lack of calibration knowledge prevents the officer being a trained operator
Application of Denneny v Harding and Mayon v DPP
CPR requirements for skeleton arguments and authority bundles on case stated appeals

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's Law Society complaint response protected by absolute privilege
key_facts: Mr G instructed solicitor Mr Avadis in family proceedings for contact and parental responsibility but terminated the retainer and complained to the Law Society/OSS.
Avadis wrote two letters to the OSS stating Mr G suffered from mental illness and doubting he would obtain contact given his conduct and mental health.
Mr G sued for defamation and fraud, alleging Avadis had fraudulently failed to apply for PR while representing that he was doing so.
Tugendhat J held the OSS letters absolutely privileged and struck out the fraud claim; permission to appeal was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal (second appeal) from High Court rulings on absolute privilege and strike-out.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on both absolute privilege and fraud strike-out.
enrichment.ratio: Communications by a solicitor to the Office for the Supervision of Solicitors in response to a regulatory inquiry are protected by absolute privilege because the OSS exercises functions sufficiently analogous to a court of justice; failure to apply for parental responsibility, even if admitted, is not a sufficient basis to plead fraud without particularised dishonesty.
legal_issues: Whether the OSS is a tribunal analogous to a court for absolute privilege purposes
Whether letters to the OSS were part of disciplinary proceedings attracting Trapp v Mackie privilege
Whether failure to apply for PR supported a fraud plea
Whether absolute privilege is compatible with Article 6

enrichment.short_title: Liquidator succeeds against director for diverting sale proceeds from insolvent IM Ltd
key_facts: MDA Investment Management Ltd (IM Ltd), a financial services company, was wound up on 23 February 2000; liquidator Mr Whalley pursued former sole director and controlling shareholder Malcolm Doney.
In July 1998 IM Ltd's business was sold to the Farlake group but part of the consideration was paid or issued to associated partnership MDA Partnership rather than to IM Ltd.
The liquidator claimed misfeasance/breach of fiduciary duty under section 212 and alternatively transactions at an undervalue under section 238 and preferences under section 239.
Park J held Doney liable in principle for misfeasance for splitting consideration, while the section 238 claim failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of liquidator's application under the Insolvency Act 1986 against director and partnership.
enrichment.outcome: Misfeasance/fiduciary breach claim succeeded in principle; section 238 claim failed; further submissions invited on quantum; Doney also liable for specified post-sale payments to related parties.
enrichment.ratio: A director who causes part of the sale consideration for an insolvent company's business to be diverted to an associated partnership rather than the company breaches fiduciary duties and commits misfeasance under section 212, even if a parallel section 238 undervalue claim fails on its particular facts.
legal_issues: Whether splitting Farlake sale consideration between IM Ltd and MDA Partnership was misfeasance or breach of fiduciary duty
Whether the transaction was a transaction at an undervalue under section 238
Whether post-sale payments to MDA Partnership, BC Ltd, and connected persons were recoverable
Quantification of Doney's liability including his partnership share

enrichment.short_title: POCA 2002 section 328 disclosure obligations in matrimonial ancillary relief
key_facts: In divorce proceedings the wife's lawyers suspected part of matrimonial assets exceeding £19 million might be criminal property derived from tax evasion.
They made authorised disclosures to NCIS under section 328 and sought urgent ex parte guidance because NCIS initially advised them not to tell client, husband, or the court.
The listed Financial Dispute Resolution was vacated; NCIS later gave appropriate consent under section 335.
The court heard submissions from parties, NCIS, Inland Revenue, Law Society, and Bar Council on POCA's impact on ancillary relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Ex parte then inter partes application in High Court Family Division for directions and declarations on POCA compliance in ancillary relief.
enrichment.outcome: Court gave guidance on section 328 authorised disclosures and consent periods; held legal advisers may inform client and opponent under sections 333/342 professional exemptions; declarations granted permitting disclosure of NCIS report.
enrichment.ratio: Negotiating or pursuing a financial remedies arrangement may amount to becoming concerned in a section 328 arrangement if criminal property is suspected, requiring authorised disclosure and appropriate consent before continuing; the tipping-off and prejudicing-investigation offences do not prevent solicitors telling their client or the other side about a disclosure when done in connection with legal advice or proceedings unless the adviser acts with intention of furthering a criminal purpose.
legal_issues: When family lawyers must make section 328 authorised disclosures in ancillary relief
Effect of section 335 notice and moratorium periods on FDR and settlement negotiations
Whether sections 333 and 342 prevent informing client or opponent of NCIS disclosure
Interaction between POCA and the duty of full and frank disclosure in financial remedy proceedings
Whether Francis v Francis construction applies to tipping-off exemptions

notes: Complete judicial review judgment on Article 6 and confiscation enforcement delay.

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 reasonable time applies to commitment for confiscation order default
key_facts: Lloyd was convicted in 1996 of conspiracy to handle stolen goods and a confiscation order of £33,326 was made with 18 months' default imprisonment.
After partial payment enforcement stalled for years; a receiver appointed in 1999 did nothing; a commitment summons was not heard until October 2002.
District Judge Evans refused to stay proceedings for delay and issued a warrant for 443 days' imprisonment; a certificate of inadequacy later reduced the sum outstanding to £8,000.
The Divisional Court held Article 6.1's reasonable time guarantee applies to commitment proceedings and stayed them for breach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' court refusal to stay commitment proceedings for delay following confiscation order enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; commitment proceedings stayed as remedy for breach of Article 6.1; imprisonment in default no longer available.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings before magistrates to commit a defendant to prison for non-payment of a confiscation order are part of the criminal proceedings attracting Article 6.1, including the reasonable time requirement; unexplained multi-year delay by enforcement authorities can violate that right and may properly be remedied by staying commitment proceedings even though the confiscation order itself remains enforceable by civil means.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6.1 reasonable time applies to commitment for confiscation default
Whether delay is attributable to the defendant's continuing duty to pay
Effect of R v Chichester Justices ex p Crowther after the Human Rights Act 1998
Appropriate remedy under section 8 HRA for breach of Article 6.1
